summary: A 1977 specification of NETRJS, a remote job entry protocol for sending batch jobs to a remote computer and getting results back. It replaced RFC 599 and is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: You hand a stack of work to a distant machine and get the answers back. NETRJS defines the steps.

subtitle: How UCLA's batch computer took jobs and returned printed output over the ARPANET, using virtual card readers and printers.

tldr.problem: Remote users wanted to submit batch jobs to a large IBM 360 Model 91 at UCLA and get their output back over the network.
tldr.mechanism: A user process acts as a Virtual Remote Batch Terminal: a Telnet console connection carries commands, and separate simplex channels carry card reader, printer and punch data in framed transactions.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is marked Historic. It replaced RFC 599 and describes the CCN service as it stood in 1977.

today: The status of RFC 740 is Historic. It obsoletes RFC 599 and RFC 189, and no later RFC is listed as replacing it.

sections.title: Virtual Remote Batch Terminals
sections.content:
NETRJS is a private protocol defined and implemented by the UCLA Campus Computing Network (CCN) for submitting batch jobs to an IBM 360 Model 91. The server gives remote users access to CCN's Remote Job Service (RJS). A NETRJS user process simulates a Virtual Remote Batch Terminal (VRBT), which can have virtual card readers, printers and punches, plus a virtual remote operator console.

A card reader sends card images and job control language to the host, jobs run by priority, and print and punch output returns to the VRBT that submitted them. A user can wait or sign off and come back later. Terminals are identified by 8-character terminal ids assigned by the server site.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer pretends to be a card reader and printer at a distant computer center, and the center sends the printouts back.

sections.title: Connections and Session Start
sections.content:
The protocol uses up to five connections. The operator console is a full-duplex Telnet connection, and the card reader, printer and punch each use a separate simplex data channel. The server only listens when channels open. All data channels use an 8-bit byte size.

A session starts with an ICP to a contact socket: 71 for EBCDIC, 73 for ASCII-68 or 75 for ASCII-63. NETRJS sends a READY message, and the user must enter SIGNON terminal-id within 3 minutes or the server closes the console. If S is the even socket sent in the ICP, the console uses S and S+1, the card reader S+2, the printer S+3 and the punch S+5. SIGNOFF waits for output in progress, then closes everything.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on one of three doors, depending on the alphabet you use. Then you say who you are, and the other channels open as you need them.

sections.title: Sending Jobs and Receiving Output
sections.content:
For input, the user opens the card reader channel, sends records of at most 80 characters, and ends the job stack with an End-of-Data transaction. The server confirms each spooled job on the console, closes the channel, and aborts it after 5 minutes of silence. On an error, it closes the channel and says the job was discarded.

For output, the VRBT opens the printer or punch channel and NETRJS sends records, the first holding the 8-character job name. Printer records start with an ASA carriage control character, and a virtual printer has 254 columns. After each job's End-of-Data the server closes the channel, so the user reopens it for the next job. The commands BSP and RST repeat output, and a job's output is discarded only after the last message is acknowledged.

The operator console takes commands such as STATUS, SET, DEFER, RESET, ROUTE and ABORT. Output waits in an Active Queue, sent at once when a channel opens, or a Deferred Queue, which must be called for by job name. Console input lines over 133 characters are truncated.
sections.plainLanguage: You feed in a stack of punched cards, then tell the center you are done. The printouts come back one job at a time, and you can ask for a page again.

sections.title: The Data Transfer Format
sections.content:
Records travel in transactions of at most 880 bytes. Each begins with a 72-bit header starting with X'FF', holding a filler count, a 16-bit sequence number starting at 0 and a 32-bit length in bits, and ending with X'00'. A stream ends with X'FE' End-of-Data unless the sender aborts. Records are either COMPRESSED, which replaces blanks or repeated characters with counts, or TRUNCATED, which drops trailing blanks. Each record begins with an op code byte that includes the channel.

Error detection is limited to the op code byte and the sequence number, and a transfer error must abort the whole transmission, with no restart.
sections.plainLanguage: Data goes in numbered boxes, each with a label saying how much is inside. If a box is lost or damaged, they stop and start over.
